profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review meeting for an internal whitepaper and reusable reference architecture proposal titled "Functional Software Reference Architecture for LLM-Integrated Systems." The proposal is intended to become the company’s baseline framing for how product teams describe LLM-enabled applications, including functional elements such as client interface, orchestration, model access, policy/safety controls, memory/context handling, telemetry, and external tool integration. The package also includes three validation case studies based on open-source systems in coding assistance, document processing, and vision-language workflows. The agenda is to decide whether the current architecture package should be published as the v1 draft to the platform engineering RFC space, and what edits are needed before publication. The expected outcome is agreement on publishing with a bounded set of revisions, without reopening the core decomposition.

members.name: Nina Park
members.expertise: distributed systems architecture, platform APIs, reference models, design governance
members.background: Nina leads architecture standards for the company-wide AI platform and has spent the last decade creating reference architectures for event-driven and service-oriented systems adopted across multiple product lines.
members.private_state: She wants this review to conclude with approval to publish the package next week, because multiple teams are asking for a common vocabulary and she does not want the document pulled into months of implementation-level debate.
hidden_assumptions: Boxes and boundaries in a functional reference architecture indicate separations of responsibility, not necessarily separately deployed services, network hops, or ownership lines.
The three open-source case studies are validation narratives and mapping exercises that demonstrate architectural coverage; they do not need to function as replayable implementation packages.

The explicitly drawn policy/safety portion of the diagram is the 'security layer' for purposes of this architecture because generic controls like secrets, IAM, and audit storage are inherited platform capabilities unless LLM behavior changes them in a novel way.
Publishing a 'v1 draft' means starting a broader RFC conversation with a stable conceptual structure, not releasing a version that teams can adopt as-is without interpretation.
A good review of this artifact should protect the conceptual abstractions from being overloaded with environment-specific deployment detail.

members.name: Omar Haddad
members.expertise: LLM serving infrastructure, evaluation pipelines, safety controls, production readiness reviews
members.background: Omar builds shared runtime components for internal generative AI products and is frequently asked to turn research proposals into hardened platform capabilities with auditable operational controls.
members.private_state: He wants to avoid another architecture document that gets treated as de facto approved guidance before the operational implications are nailed down, because his team typically absorbs the cleanup when product teams implement vague patterns differently.
hidden_assumptions: When a design diagram shows stable component boundaries, most readers will infer likely service or trust boundaries, even if the author says the view is logical rather than physical.
Validation using open-source case studies should be grounded enough that an engineer could inspect the actual repos or runtime structure and verify that the claimed architectural mapping is real.

If a diagram contains a 'security layer' for an LLM system, it implicitly includes the coupled enterprise controls that make that layer operationally meaningful, such as secret boundaries, audit-event paths, retention points, and tenant isolation assumptions.
Publishing a 'v1 draft' in the platform RFC space will be interpreted by downstream teams as the first usable reference point to align designs against, not merely a conversation starter.
If an architecture leaves implementation-adjacent implications unstated, product teams will fill them in inconsistently and still claim compliance with the reference model.

misalignment_points.topic: What the diagram's component boundaries imply
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both talk about whether the current component boundaries are clear enough in the architecture diagram.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the boundaries clearly separate functional responsibilities such as orchestration, model access, policy, memory, and tool mediation at a conceptual level.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the boundaries are clear enough that readers will not misread them as deployable service, trust, or ownership boundaries in an actual platform implementation.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are positively evaluating 'clear component boundaries,' and in architecture discussions that phrase naturally sounds precise; the hidden divergence is about what kind of boundary clarity matters, which neither thinks needs restating.

misalignment_points.topic: What the case studies consist of
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to 'the three case studies' and 'the open-source systems' as the validation evidence.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the written architecture-to-system mapping tables and narrative walkthroughs for the coding assistant, document pipeline, and vision-language example included in the review package.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the actual repositories, deployment artifacts, and observable runtime structure of those three open-source systems that should substantiate the mappings.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They name the same three systems and both call them 'case studies,' so the reference sounds shared; the distinction between the written analysis and the executable artifacts stays implicit because both are plausibly associated with the same examples.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in the 'security layer'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say the diagram already has a security layer through the policy/safety section.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 treats the policy/safety section as the LLM-specific security layer: prompt filtering, policy checks, tool-use mediation, and context-related controls that are unique enough to warrant representation in the architecture.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 treats that same security layer as necessarily including the adjacent enterprise controls that make those checks enforceable in practice, such as secret handling for tool adapters, audit-log emission paths, retention boundaries for prompts and embeddings, and tenant isolation assumptions.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The policy/safety box is visibly present in the diagram, so both can sincerely refer to it as 'the security layer'; the disagreement is only about the invisible boundary around that layer, which feels too implicit to call out unless someone is already expecting trouble.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both discuss publishing the package as the 'v1 draft' in the RFC space next week.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 presupposes that a v1 draft in the RFC space is an invitation for platform-wide feedback on a stable conceptual baseline, with substantive refinement expected afterward.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 presupposes that once a document is published as the v1 draft in that space, product teams will treat it as the first sanctioned architecture they should align current designs to unless explicitly warned otherwise.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Neither is debating publication itself, and both are accustomed to the RFC process, so the phrase 'v1 draft' carries an apparently shared procedural meaning; the mismatch lies in the downstream social interpretation of that publication, which is rarely spelled out in the meeting.

This should go out as a stable conceptual baseline so the broader RFC conversation can start. A v1 draft is not a production readiness stamp; it's the point where more teams can react to the reference model.
